The year the river forgot its voice, I was sent to Shanyang County to take a dead man’s place.

My name is Li Wen, clerk of the Ministry of Works, third rank by stubbornness and fourth by talent. When the summons arrived, it carried the red seal of the prefect and the smell of damp paper—ink that had drunk too long in a drawer. It ordered me to travel east and oversee the repair of the Grand Canal’s stone locks near Shanyang. The previous inspector, Master Qiu, had died at his desk, brush still in hand, as if his heart had been commanded to stop mid-stroke.

Such deaths are not uncommon in the capital. Men sit for too long in the posture of obedience and forget how to rise. Yet the prefect’s letter ended with a line that did not sound like the language of officials:

*Do not go out after the second watch. Do not answer if you hear your name spoken in the courtyard.*

I laughed, because laughter is the easiest shield a scholar owns. Then I packed my inkstone, my seal, my winter robe, and a small volume of the *Book of Songs* my mother had wrapped in cloth as though it were medicine.

The road to Shanyang was a gray ribbon between fields flattened by last season’s floods. Peasants bent in mud like punctuation marks in a sentence the heavens had not finished. The canal itself ran alongside the road for days—broad, patient, and strangely silent. Even where the wind passed over it, there was no ripple, as if the water had learned to hold its breath.

When I reached the county yamen at dusk, the doorkeeper took my travel pass without meeting my eyes. He led me through a courtyard where the stone lions had been rubbed smooth by decades of hands seeking luck. The lanterns were lit early, their light thin as rice gruel.

The magistrate, Lord Huang, received me in a room that smelled of old cedar and newer fear. He was a round man whose official hat sat too tightly on his head, as though it had been tied there.

“Clerk Li,” he said, “you have come quickly.”

“I have been ordered,” I replied.

“That is how we all come.” He rubbed at a spot on his sleeve that wasn’t there. “You will sleep in the eastern guest quarters.”

“The quarters used by Master Qiu?”

A pause, brief as the blink of a carp. “Yes.”

“And his papers?”

“They are sealed.” His voice thinned. “We will open them tomorrow.”

It was not my place to ask more. Still, as I followed a servant through corridors, I said, lightly, “In the capital they say Shanyang is haunted. What does the countryside call a ghost these days?”

The servant’s shoulders tightened beneath his cotton coat. “We call it what it calls itself,” he murmured, and hurried on.

My quarters faced the canal. A small stone bridge arched nearby, elegant as a scholar’s eyebrow. Beyond it, reeds stood in black clumps, and above them the sky lay flat and cold.

Inside, the room was clean, too clean, as though the air had been scrubbed. A single writing table stood by the window. On it sat an inkstone, already filled, and a brush with its tip dipped in dry black.

I had not brought my own brush out yet.

I looked to the servant. “Who prepared these?”

He shook his head quickly. “They were… already.”

When he left, I stood for a long time listening to the house settle. An official residence always groans and sighs at night—wood remembering the trees it once was. But this place made a different sound, a faint scratching like a rat behind paper.

It came from the table.

I moved closer. On the table’s surface, just beside the inkstone, lay a sheet of yellowed paper. It had not been there a moment ago—I would have sworn it. Written on it in careful clerical script were four characters:

**回头看水**  
*Turn your head. Look at the water.*

My breath cooled. A trick, I told myself. The magistrate’s men, perhaps, testing a new inspector to see whether he was easily frightened.

Still, my neck refused to move.

Outside the window, the canal lay dark and flat. The second watch drum sounded somewhere within the yamen—two measured beats swallowed by mist.

In the capital we pride ourselves on reason, as if reason were a lamp that could be carried anywhere. Yet when the world grows dim enough, the lamp only makes the darkness around it more obvious.

I turned my head.

At first there was only the canal, and my own pale reflection ghosting in the glass. Then the water shifted as if someone beneath it had exhaled. A circle widened, perfectly round, as if drawn with a compass. Another circle touched it. Another. The ripples were not random; they formed strokes.

On the surface of the canal, written in water that held its shape, appeared a single character:

**冤**  
*Wronged.*

The ripples stilled. The character remained, shining faintly in the moon’s thin light, and then sank as if absorbed.

My mouth had gone dry. I stepped back from the window, and my heel struck something soft. I looked down.

A pair of shoes lay behind me. Not mine. Official shoes, black with embroidered borders, neatly placed as if the owner had stepped out of them and vanished into air. The soles were damp.

I did not touch them. I sat on the edge of my bed and kept my hands in my sleeves like a child in winter.

That was my first night in Shanyang.

It was not the last.

---

The next morning Lord Huang unsealed Master Qiu’s papers in the main hall. The wax seal cracked with a sound like a bone snapping. Inside were routine reports: lists of stones, measurements, labor counts, all written with the dull precision of a man counting his own days.

Then, folded within the last report, was a separate sheet. It bore no official header. Its ink was darker, as if the brush had been dipped in something thicker than water.

Master Qiu had written:

*The locks do not fail because the stones are weak. They fail because the river is hungry.*

*At night I hear the canal reciting names.*

*If I die at my desk, know that I did not fall asleep.*

Lord Huang’s face had gone pale in a way that made him look suddenly older, as if the fear had been waiting beneath his skin and had finally been called forth.

“This is nonsense,” he said quickly. “A man’s imagination, inflamed by damp air.”

“Yet he is dead,” I said.

The magistrate’s eyes flicked toward the open doors, where the courtyard light lay like a thin cloth. “He worked late. He—his heart was weak.”

I did not argue. Instead, I asked to inspect the locks.

Lord Huang hesitated. “In daylight, you may go.”

In daylight.

As if ghosts, like petty thieves, could be kept out by the sun.

---

The canal locks at Shanyang were ancient, older than the oldest men in the market. Great stones fitted together like teeth. They should have held. Yet along the seams, the mortar had cracked and oozed a fine black sand that looked like ground ink.

The foreman, a leathery man named Xu, showed me the damage. “We repair,” he said, “and the next morning it is as if hands have pulled the stones apart again.”

“Hands?” I repeated.

Xu spat into the dirt. “If you ask my men, they will tell you it is the drowned ones. The canal takes and takes.”

“How many have drowned here?”

He stared out at the water, his eyes narrowing against the daylight. “When the floods came last year, the water rose faster than prayers. Whole houses went under. People climbed trees. People climbed each other. The canal did not care.”

“And the dead?”

“The dead floated down to the next county,” he said. “Or they did not float at all.”

As we walked along the bank, I saw scraps of cloth snagged in reeds—faded sleeves, a child’s sash—trophies the water had kept. The air smelled of wet stone and something else, sweet and rotting beneath it.

When we reached the small arched bridge near my quarters, Xu stopped.

“This is where Master Qiu liked to stand,” he said. “He would watch the water as if waiting for it to speak.”

“Did it?”

Xu glanced at me sideways. “At night,” he said, “it speaks like a magistrate. It calls names.”

My skin tightened along my arms. “Whose names?”

“Sometimes the names of the drowned. Sometimes…” He swallowed. “Sometimes the names of the living.”

---

That evening, I lit incense and placed it on the window ledge. The smoke curled into the room, a thin gray dragon seeking a way out.

I told myself this was for propriety. Officials should show respect to local spirits. It was not fear.

The second watch drum sounded.

I sat at the table with my own inkstone now, my own brush. The foreign brush that had been waiting the night before lay in the corner, its hairs stiff as if with old blood.

I began to write my report, describing the locks, the cracks, the need for more stone and labor. Ordinary words, heavy as bricks.

Halfway through a sentence, the candle flame bent sharply to the left, as though someone had passed by.

Then a voice spoke outside the window, soft as silk pulled slowly through rings.

“Li Wen.”

My brush froze, a drop of ink swelling at its tip. My name, spoken with the exact tone my mother used when calling me in from the courtyard as a child—affection laced with impatience.

The prefect’s warning returned to me like a hand on the back of my neck: *Do not answer if you hear your name spoken in the courtyard.*

I did not respond.

The voice sighed, a sound that could have been wind. “Li Wen.”

The courtyard outside was empty, lanterns burning steadily. The canal lay beyond, black and still.

I forced myself to keep writing, though the characters came crooked.

“Li Wen,” the voice said a third time, closer now, as if the speaker stood just outside the door.

I gripped my brush so tightly my fingers ached. Silence, I told myself. Silence is the gate a ghost cannot pass.

There was a pause. Then, from the table itself, a scratching sound began, as if an invisible brush moved across paper.

My eyes dropped.

A sheet of paper lay beside my report—blank a moment before. Now black ink bloomed across it in flowing strokes, written by no hand I could see.

**借你一笔**  
*Borrow your brush.*

The brush in my hand jerked, pulled as though by a tug at its hairs. I nearly dropped it. The ink in my stone rippled.

A coldness seeped up through the table into my wrists. The candle dimmed, though no wind touched it.

On the blank sheet, characters continued to appear, swift and elegant, as if written by a practiced scholar.

**我名邱文正**  
*My name is Qiu Wenzheng.*

Master Qiu.

The candle flame steadied suddenly, as if satisfied.

My throat tightened. I forced myself to whisper, not an answer to a voice outside, but words to the ink in front of me. “Why do you write?”

The brush in my hand lifted slightly, as if the unseen writer considered.

On the paper:

**不能说，只能写。**  
*I cannot speak. I can only write.*

I swallowed. “Why did you die?”

The ink darkened, the strokes pressing hard enough to dent the paper.

**他们把我的口封在水里。**  
*They sealed my mouth in the water.*

The room seemed to tilt. Outside, the canal gave a faint sound at last—not a ripple, but something like a distant throat clearing.

I stared at the words until my eyes burned. “Who are ‘they’?”

The brush hesitated, then wrote slowly, as if each stroke cost effort.

**官与水，一样重。**  
*Officials and water are equally heavy.*

I felt my face heat with anger—anger at superstition, at implication, at the lazy poetry of ghosts. “If you mean the magistrate—”

The candle flared, then guttered. In the brief brightening, I saw something on the window glass.

A wet handprint.

Long fingers. The palm too large. Water beading and running down like tears.

Then the light died to a trembling thread, and in the dark I heard the canal speak—not in words, but in the rhythm of a brush on paper.

Scratch. Scratch.

As if the entire riverbank were a writing desk.

I did not sleep.

---

Over the next days, I became careful with my questions.

When I addressed Master Qiu, I did so by writing, not speaking. I laid paper on the table at dusk and left my brush there. Sometimes the brush moved; sometimes it did not. Sometimes I found words at dawn like insects caught in ink.

What I learned came in fragments.

Shanyang had flooded because the locks had been tampered with. The stones, once fitted tightly, had been loosened. The mortar had been cut and replaced with a mixture that dissolved in water like rice paper.

The flood had killed hundreds.

Then relief grain meant for the survivors had been diverted, sold, and its profits split. Names appeared on my paper: the foreman Xu, two local gentry, an assistant magistrate. Lord Huang’s own name was written once, the strokes shaky, as if even the ghost hesitated to accuse a man with a seal.

And always, beneath the names, the same character appeared:

**冤.**  
*Wronged.*

It was not Master Qiu who was haunting the canal, I began to understand. He was only the newest ink in an older stain.

The canal itself had become a mouth for those denied one.

In ancient times, they say wronged spirits cling to places where their blood fell. Here, there had been no blood—only water. So the spirits clung to the river’s surface, to the locks, to the bridge, to the damp shoes left behind.

One night, as I sat with my hands tucked in my sleeves, the brush wrote:

**明夜三更，桥下。带印。**  
*Tomorrow night, third watch, under the bridge. Bring your seal.*

My seal.

The small piece of carved jade I used to authenticate reports, to make words official. In the capital, a man’s seal is his authority. Without it, his writing is merely complaint.

A ghost wanted my authority.

My first thought was to refuse. My second was that refusal is a luxury for men who are not already standing at the edge of a river that knows their name.

---

The third watch came with fog. The world narrowed to lantern light and the damp sound of my own breath. I wrapped my robe tighter and stepped into the courtyard.

Every instinct screamed to stay inside, to obey the prefect’s warning. Yet I had already broken it by listening, by reading, by letting ink move where it wished.

The bridge lay ahead, a pale arch in the mist. The canal beneath it was darker than the night around it, as if the water had stolen the fog and stored it.

I walked to the bridge and stopped.

Under the arch, something moved.

At first I thought it was reeds swaying. Then it rose, slowly, as though the water were pushing up a shape it had been hiding.

A man stood beneath the bridge, waist-deep in the canal, as if the water were solid enough to hold him. His official robe clung to him in long wet folds. His hat sat crooked. His face was pallid, swollen slightly, the way drowned faces are described in old cases.

His eyes were open.

When he looked at me, I felt the pressure of the gaze not on my skin but on my bones, like cold fingers searching for a crack.

I knew without being told: Master Qiu.

He lifted his hands.

His sleeves dripped steadily, making a soft, patient sound. *Plink. Plink.* Like a clerk counting coins.

He opened his mouth.

No sound came out.

Then, from the canal itself, a voice rose—not his, but many layered together, as though a hundred throats spoke through one waterlogged instrument.

“Seal.”

The fog around the bridge thickened. The lanterns along the path behind me dimmed, their light withdrawing as if afraid.

My hand went to the pouch at my waist. The jade seal was there, cool, familiar. In the capital it had felt like a tool. Here it felt like bait.

“What do you want?” I asked, though my voice shook.

The water-voice answered, slow and heavy:

“Write.”

Master Qiu raised a sheet of paper above the canal. It should have dissolved, but it remained intact, pale in the dim light. The brush in his other hand—my brush, I saw with a jolt, its handle marked by my thumbprint—hovered above the paper.

The paper was blank.

“Write what?” I whispered.

The water-voice spoke my name the way my mother had, and the bridge stones seemed to lean closer to listen.

“Li Wen,” it said, “make it official.”

My stomach tightened. I understood then what the ghost meant. A report. An accusation stamped with my seal. A document that could travel up the hierarchy like a fish swimming against current.

In daylight, such a report would be “reviewed,” “considered,” “delayed.” Names might be crossed out. Phrases softened. The truth could be folded into nothing.

But here, under a bridge, in fog, with the dead watching, the words would not be for the living alone.

“If I do,” I said, “they will kill me.”

Master Qiu’s eyes did not change. Dead eyes do not widen. But the water around him stirred, and the voice answered, almost gently:

“Then you will join us. And you will not be alone.”

The fog cooled my face. I tasted river water though my mouth was closed.

For a moment I thought of my mother’s hands wrapping the *Book of Songs* in cloth. Of my father’s pride when I passed the examinations. Of the way officials in the capital talk about the people as though they are numbers carved on abacus beads.

I thought of the character that had risen from the canal like a truth refusing to drown.

**冤.**

I took out my seal.

“Give me the paper,” I said.

Master Qiu lifted it higher. The brush extended toward me, hovering. I reached out.

His hand was not cold.

It was wet, yes, but it had the warmth of a living body just returned from a bath. That warmth frightened me more than any chill. It suggested not decay, but persistence.

I took the brush.

My fingers tightened around it.

The water beneath the bridge shivered with anticipation. The fog pressed in.

On the paper, I began to write.

Not poetry. Not hints. Names, dates, amounts of grain diverted, the method of tampering with the locks. I wrote of the flood, the bodies, the cloth in reeds. I wrote as an official, because only an official’s words could pierce an official’s armor.

When I finished, my hand was cramped and my sleeve soaked to the elbow, though I did not recall dipping the brush.

I pressed my jade seal into the ink Master Qiu held out—an ink that was not from my stone, blacker than night.

Then I stamped the paper.

The red imprint bloomed like fresh blood.

The moment the seal lifted, the canal gave its first true sound since I had arrived: a deep rushing, as though it had been holding back its own flow and had finally been permitted to run.

Fog tore away in strips. The lanterns behind me flared back to life.

Master Qiu’s mouth moved. For the first time, a whisper escaped—not from the canal, but from him.

“Thank you,” he breathed, and the word was thin as rice paper.

Then his body folded, sinking into the water without splash, as if the canal were accepting back what had been borrowed.

The stamped document did not sink.

It floated up onto the surface, drifting toward the center of the canal as though carried by an invisible hand. The current, which had been still, now bore it away, upstream—against the direction water should travel.

Toward the capital.

I stood on the bridge until my legs trembled.

When I finally returned to my quarters, my table was bare. The foreign brush was gone. Master Qiu’s damp shoes were gone.

Only my own inkstone remained, and beside it a single character written on a fresh sheet of paper in my own hand, though I did not remember writing it:

**慎.**  
*Be careful.*

---

The next morning Lord Huang was arrested.

Not by my doing. Not directly.

A courier arrived from the prefecture, breathless, carrying an edict and a copy of an accusation that bore my seal.

“How—” Lord Huang began, when the guards presented it.

His eyes fixed on the red imprint. His face drained of color as though the seal had sucked it out.

He turned to me, and for the first time since my arrival, his eyes met mine fully.

“Clerk Li,” he whispered, “what have you done?”

Before I could answer, the courier added, “The accusation arrived last night. It was found on the steps of the prefect’s hall at the third watch, dry as bone. No one saw who delivered it.”

Lord Huang made a sound like a man choking on his own name.

They led him away.

The assistant magistrate fled and was caught two days later hiding in a grain store. Foreman Xu disappeared. Some said he drowned; others said he made it to the coast. The gentry burned incense and pretended they had always advocated honesty.

Work on the locks began in earnest. Stones were replaced. Mortar was mixed properly. Laborers were paid. Grain was distributed under watchful eyes.

The canal, slowly, began to speak again in the normal way water speaks—by moving.

Yet even as life returned to its usual patterns, I could not shake the feeling that the canal was watching, waiting to see if the living would forget.

On my last night in Shanyang, as I packed my belongings, I opened my mother’s cloth-wrapped book and read a poem at random.

*The river is wide; how shall I cross?  
With bundles of reeds, with little boats…*

Outside, the canal lapped softly against the bank. A night bird called once and fell silent. The air smelled of mud and pine smoke.

I tied my seal carefully into its pouch.

Then, as I extinguished the lamp, I heard a voice—not in the courtyard this time, but in the water beyond the window. It did not speak my name. It did not ask for anything.

It only recited, low and steady, like a clerk reading a ledger aloud:

Names.

Dozens of them. Some I recognized from the flood records. Some I did not. The cadence was calm, inexhaustible.

As if the canal were reminding me of the price it had been forced to collect.

I sat in darkness and listened until the fourth watch, when the voice faded into the ordinary sound of moving water.

In the morning, the canal was bright under the winter sun, full of boats and shouting men. Children ran along the bank with paper kites. Life looked so loud and solid that I might have believed the haunting had been a dream.

But as my cart crossed the small arched bridge on the road out of Shanyang, I glanced down.

For an instant

On the blank sheet, characters continued to appear, swift and elegant, as if written by a practiced scholar.

**我名邱文正**  
*My name is Qiu Wenzheng.*

Master Qiu.

The candle flame steadied suddenly, as if satisfied.

My throat tightened. I forced myself to whisper, not an answer to a voice outside, but words to the ink in front of me. “Why do you write?”

The brush in my hand lifted slightly, as if the unseen writer considered.

On the paper:

**不能说，只能写。**  
*I cannot speak. I can only write.*

I swallowed. “Why did you die?”

The ink darkened, the strokes pressing hard enough to dent the paper.

**他们把我的口封在水里。**  
*They sealed my mouth in the water.*

The room seemed to tilt. Outside, the canal gave a faint sound at last—not a ripple, but something like a distant throat clearing.

I stared at the words until my eyes burned. “Who are ‘they’?”

The brush hesitated, then wrote slowly, as if each stroke cost effort.

**官与水，一样重。**  
*Officials and water are equally heavy.*

I felt my face heat with anger—anger at superstition, at implication, at the lazy poetry of ghosts. “If you mean the magistrate—”

The candle flared, then guttered. In the brief brightening, I saw something on the window glass.

A wet handprint.

Long fingers. The palm too large. Water beading and running down like tears.

Then the light died to a trembling thread, and in the dark I heard the canal speak—not in words, but in the rhythm of a brush on paper.

Scratch. Scratch.

As if the entire riverbank were a writing desk.

I did not sleep.

---

Over the next days, I became careful with my questions.

When I addressed Master Qiu, I did so by writing, not speaking. I laid paper on the table at dusk and left my brush there. Sometimes the brush moved; sometimes it did not. Sometimes I found words at dawn like insects caught in ink.

What I learned came in fragments.

Shanyang had flooded because the locks had been tampered with. The stones, once fitted tightly, had been loosened. The mortar had been cut and replaced with a mixture that dissolved in water like rice paper.

The flood had killed hundreds.

Then relief grain meant for the survivors had been diverted, sold, and its profits split. Names appeared on my paper: the foreman Xu, two local gentry, an assistant magistrate. Lord Huang’s own name was written once, the strokes shaky, as if even the ghost hesitated to accuse a man with a seal.

And always, beneath the names, the same character appeared:

**冤.**  
*Wronged.*

It was not Master Qiu who was haunting the canal, I began to understand. He was only the newest ink in an older stain.

The canal itself had become a mouth for those denied one.

In ancient times, they say wronged spirits cling to places where their blood fell. Here, there had been no blood—only water. So the spirits clung to the river’s surface, to the locks, to the bridge, to the damp shoes left behind.

One night, as I sat with my hands tucked in my sleeves, the brush wrote:

**明夜三更，桥下。带印。**  
*Tomorrow night, third watch, under the bridge. Bring your seal.*

My seal.

The small piece of carved jade I used to authenticate reports, to make words official. In the capital, a man’s seal is his authority. Without it, his writing is merely complaint.

A ghost wanted my authority.

My first thought was to refuse. My second was that refusal is a luxury for men who are not already standing at the edge of a river that knows their name.

---

The third watch came with fog. The world narrowed to lantern light and the damp sound of my own breath. I wrapped my robe tighter and stepped into the courtyard.

Every instinct screamed to stay inside, to obey the prefect’s warning. Yet I had already broken it by listening, by reading, by letting ink move where it wished.

The bridge lay ahead, a pale arch in the mist. The canal beneath it was darker than the night around it, as if the water had stolen the fog and stored it.

I walked to the bridge and stopped.

Under the arch, something moved.

At first I thought it was reeds swaying. Then it rose, slowly, as though the water were pushing up a shape it had been hiding.

A man stood beneath the bridge, waist-deep in the canal, as if the water were solid enough to hold him. His official robe clung to him in long wet folds. His hat sat crooked. His face was pallid, swollen slightly, the way drowned faces are described in old cases.

His eyes were open.

When he looked at me, I felt the pressure of the gaze not on my skin but on my bones, like cold fingers searching for a crack.

I knew without being told: Master Qiu.

He lifted his hands.

His sleeves dripped steadily, making a soft, patient sound. *Plink. Plink.* Like a clerk counting coins.

He opened his mouth.

No sound came out.

Then, from the canal itself, a voice rose—not his, but many layered together, as though a hundred throats spoke through one waterlogged instrument.

“Seal.”

The fog around the bridge thickened. The lanterns along the path behind me dimmed, their light withdrawing as if afraid.

My hand went to the pouch at my waist. The jade seal was there, cool, familiar. In the capital it had felt like a tool. Here it felt like bait.

“What do you want?” I asked, though my voice shook.

The water-voice answered, slow and heavy:

“Write.”

Master Qiu raised a sheet of paper above the canal. It should have dissolved, but it remained intact, pale in the dim light. The brush in his other hand—my brush, I saw with a jolt, its handle marked by my thumbprint—hovered above the paper.

The paper was blank.

“Write what?” I whispered.

The water-voice spoke my name the way my mother had, and the bridge stones seemed to lean closer to listen.

“Li Wen,” it said, “make it official.”

My stomach tightened. I understood then what the ghost meant. A report. An accusation stamped with my seal. A document that could travel up the hierarchy like a fish swimming against current.

In daylight, such a report would be “reviewed,” “considered,” “delayed.” Names might be crossed out. Phrases softened. The truth could be folded into nothing.

But here, under a bridge, in fog, with the dead watching, the words would not be for the living alone.

“If I do,” I said, “they will kill me.”

Master Qiu’s eyes did not change. Dead eyes do not widen. But the water around him stirred, and the voice answered, almost gently:

“Then you will join us. And you will not be alone.”

The fog cooled my face. I tasted river water though my mouth was closed.

For a moment I thought of my mother’s hands wrapping the *Book of Songs* in cloth. Of my father’s pride when I passed the examinations. Of the way officials in the capital talk about the people as though they are numbers carved on abacus beads.

I thought of the character that had risen from the canal like a truth refusing to drown.

**冤.**

I took out my seal.

“Give me the paper,” I said.

Master Qiu lifted it higher. The brush extended toward me, hovering. I reached out.

His hand was not cold.

It was wet, yes, but it had the warmth of a living body just returned from a bath. That warmth frightened me more than any chill. It suggested not decay, but persistence.

I took the brush.

My fingers tightened around it.

The water beneath the bridge shivered with anticipation. The fog pressed in.

On the paper, I began to write.

Not poetry. Not hints. Names, dates, amounts of grain diverted, the method of tampering with the locks. I wrote of the flood, the bodies, the cloth in reeds. I wrote as an official, because only an official’s words could pierce an official’s armor.

When I finished, my hand was cramped and my sleeve soaked to the elbow, though I did not recall dipping the brush.

I pressed my jade seal into the ink Master Qiu held out—an ink that was not from my stone, blacker than night.

Then I stamped the paper.

The red imprint bloomed like fresh blood.

The moment the seal lifted, the canal gave its first true sound since I had arrived: a deep rushing, as though it had been holding back its own flow and had finally been permitted to run.

Fog tore away in strips. The lanterns behind me flared back to life.

Master Qiu’s mouth moved. For the first time, a whisper escaped—not from the canal, but from him.

“Thank you,” he breathed, and the word was thin as rice paper.

Then his body folded, sinking into the water without splash, as if the canal were accepting back what had been borrowed.

The stamped document did not sink.

It floated up onto the surface, drifting toward the center of the canal as though carried by an invisible hand. The current, which had been still, now bore it away, upstream—against the direction water should travel.

Toward the capital.

I stood on the bridge until my legs trembled.

When I finally returned to my quarters, my table was bare. The foreign brush was gone. Master Qiu’s damp shoes were gone.

Only my own inkstone remained, and beside it a single character written on a fresh sheet of paper in my own hand, though I did not remember writing it:

**慎.**  
*Be careful.*

---

The next morning Lord Huang was arrested.

Not by my doing. Not directly.

A courier arrived from the prefecture, breathless, carrying an edict and a copy of an accusation that bore my seal.

“How—” Lord Huang began, when the guards presented it.

His eyes fixed on the red imprint. His face drained of color as though the seal had sucked it out.

He turned to me, and for the first time since my arrival, his eyes met mine fully.

“Clerk Li,” he whispered, “what have you done?”

Before I could answer, the courier added, “The accusation arrived last night. It was found on the steps of the prefect’s hall at the third watch, dry as bone. No one saw who delivered it.”

Lord Huang made a sound like a man choking on his own name.

They led him away.

The assistant magistrate fled and was caught two days later hiding in a grain store. Foreman Xu disappeared. Some said he drowned; others said he made it to the coast. The gentry burned incense and pretended they had always advocated honesty.

Work on the locks began in earnest. Stones were replaced. Mortar was mixed properly. Laborers were paid. Grain was distributed under watchful eyes.

The canal, slowly, began to speak again in the normal way water speaks—by moving.

Yet even as life returned to its usual patterns, I could not shake the feeling that the canal was watching, waiting to see if the living would forget.

On my last night in Shanyang, as I packed my belongings, I opened my mother’s cloth-wrapped book and read a poem at random.

*The river is wide; how shall I cross?  
With bundles of reeds, with little boats…*

Outside, the canal lapped softly against the bank. A night bird called once and fell silent. The air smelled of mud and pine smoke.

I tied my seal carefully into its pouch.

Then, as I extinguished the lamp, I heard a voice—not in the courtyard this time, but in the water beyond the window. It did not speak my name. It did not ask for anything.

It only recited, low and steady, like a clerk reading a ledger aloud:

Names.

Dozens of them. Some I recognized from the flood records. Some I did not. The cadence was calm, inexhaustible.

As if the canal were reminding me of the price it had been forced to collect.

I sat in darkness and listened until the fourth watch, when the voice faded into the ordinary sound of moving water.

In the morning, the canal was bright under the winter sun, full of boats and shouting men. Children ran along the bank with paper kites. Life looked so loud and solid that I might have believed the haunting had been a dream.

But as my cart crossed the small arched bridge on the road out of Shanyang, I glanced down.

For an instant
